Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Amid high emotions and tight security, thousands lined the streets of Beirut Friday to honor Antoine Ghanem, the anti-Syrian Lebanese MP killed in a powerful bomb blast along with four others. Amin Gemayel (R), Phalange party head, carries the coffin of assassinated deputy Antoine Ghamen. Against an atmosphere of intense political and patriotic fervor, the flag-draped coffins of the politician and two bodyguards also killed in Wednesday's rush hour blast made its way through the city's Christian district to the Sacred Heart church on what the government had declared as a day of national mourning. The procession was accompanied by thousands waving flags, as well as a brass band playing the anthem of Ghanem's Phalange Party, The Associated Press reported . TV pictures showed distraught mourners crowding and reaching out to the coffins as they were carried aloft. Several people were seen to collapse and had to be carried away. Mourners also carried photographs, threw rose petals and unfurled banners, some of which read "We Won't Kneel," AP said. The coffins were greeted at the Christian Maronite church with applause from the gathered mourners, the agency said, including majority leaders and the Lebanese cabinet as well as Ghanem's family and friends. Ghanem was later buried in the city's Christian district. Ghanem's death is the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, with the most notorious being the February 2005 assassination in Beirut of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, which sparked widespread protests that led to the ouster of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri also died in a massive explosion. The incident threatens to cast the country into political uncertainty ahead of a key presidential vote in a tightly divided parliament, almost evenly split between anti- and pro-Syrian camps.  Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics » . CNN's Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said that many Lebanese now feared for the future, especially given other events in the region including the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis, recent political differences in Iraq and Iran's bid to become a super power. "There continues to be among a great deal of people here a sense of foreboding that perhaps the worst is yet to come," he said. U.S. President George W. Bush, in a written statement, joined other world leaders in condemning the "horrific assassination." "Since October 2004, there has been a tragic pattern of political assassinations and attempted assassinations designed to silence those Lebanese who courageously defend their vision of an independent and democratic Lebanon," Bush said Wednesday. Also in a written statement, a spokesperson for Ban Ki-moon said the U.N. secretary-general "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack." "The secretary general urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course," the spokesperson said. Bush's statement added: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty." The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued a statement saying: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy." And U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in a written statement, said: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country," Rice said. "Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction." # Anti-Syrian Lebanese MP Antoine Ghanem Killed in Beirut Car Bombing

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — Anti-Syrian lawmaker Antoine Ghanem was killed Wednesday in a car bombing in a Christian suburb of Beirut, becoming the latest anti-Syrian figure to be assassinated in Lebanon in a wave of political violence that has shaken the country.

The explosion, which struck in the Sin el-Fil neighborhood, killed at least five other people and wounded dozens more, according to Lebanese security officials. The blast tore through the busy street, leaving mangled vehicles and shattered storefronts in its wake.

Ghanem, 64, was a member of the Christian Phalange Party and part of the parliamentary majority that has opposed Syrian influence in Lebanese affairs.

## A Blow to the Parliamentary Majority

The killing further thins the ranks of the anti-Syrian coalition in Lebanon's parliament, where the governing majority has been steadily eroded by a series of assassinations. The timing raised immediate concerns, coming just days before parliament was scheduled to convene to elect a new president.

"This is a naked attempt to intimidate the elected representatives of the Lebanese people," said one member of the March 14 coalition, referring to the pro-Western alliance that has held a slim majority.

## Funeral Procession Draws Mourners

Thousands of mourners filled the streets of Beirut for Ghanem's funeral procession, waving Lebanese flags and Phalange Party banners as the slain lawmaker's coffin was carried through the capital. Grieving supporters chanted slogans against Syria, holding photographs of Ghanem aloft.

The procession made its way through the city amid heavy security, with emotions running high among crowds who have grown weary of the violence targeting their political leaders. Family members, party officials, and ordinary citizens marched together in a display of solidarity and defiance.

Church bells tolled as religious and political figures gathered to pay their respects, transforming the funeral into both a moment of mourning and a political demonstration against those blamed for the ongoing bloodshed.

## International Condemnation

World leaders swiftly condemned the assassination.

The United States denounced the killing, with officials describing it as an attempt to derail Lebanon's democratic process. Washington called for those responsible to be brought to justice and reaffirmed support for Lebanon's sovereignty and independence.

United Nations Secretary-General officials expressed alarm at the continuing pattern of political assassinations, urging Lebanese authorities to maintain stability during the sensitive electoral period.

France, which has historically maintained close ties with Lebanon, joined in condemning the attack. European leaders echoed calls for calm and emphasized the importance of allowing Lebanon's political institutions to function without intimidation.

## A Pattern of Violence

Ghanem's assassination follows a series of similar attacks against anti-Syrian politicians and journalists in recent years. The March 14 coalition has repeatedly accused Damascus of orchestrating the killings—charges that Syria has consistently denied.

The violence has fueled political tensions in a country still recovering from years of conflict and struggling with deep divisions over its future direction and relationship with neighboring Syria.

As Lebanon prepares for the critical presidential vote, the killing has cast a shadow over the proceedings, raising fears of further instability in a nation long caught between competing regional and international pressures.

*This is a developing story.*

**BEIRUT** — Tens of thousands of mourners flooded the streets of central Beirut on Thursday for the funeral of prominent Lebanese politician and outspoken government critic, who was killed earlier this week when a powerful car bomb tore through his motorcade in a busy commercial district.

The blast, which also claimed the lives of at least three bystanders and wounded dozens more, has plunged the country into a fresh wave of political uncertainty and reignited fears of renewed instability in the fragile Mediterranean nation.

## A Sea of Mourners

Crowds gathered before dawn near Martyrs' Square, many waving Lebanese flags and holding portraits of the slain lawmaker. Religious leaders from across Lebanon's diverse sectarian communities joined the procession, which wound slowly through the capital under a heavy security presence.

"He spoke for those who had no voice," said one mourner, a schoolteacher who traveled from the north to attend. "They can silence a man, but they cannot silence an idea."

The funeral service, held at a downtown cathedral, drew government officials, foreign diplomats, and ordinary citizens alike. Church bells tolled as the coffin, draped in the national flag, was carried through the crowd amid chants demanding justice and accountability.

## International Condemnation

The assassination drew swift and forceful reactions from world leaders, many of whom framed the killing as an assault on Lebanon's sovereignty and democratic aspirations.

Speaking from Washington, President George W. Bush condemned the attack in the strongest terms.

"The United States stands with the Lebanese people in this dark hour," Bush said. "This murder is a horrific reminder of those who would use violence and terror to derail the march of freedom. We call for a full and transparent investigation, and those responsible must be held to account."

Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice echoed the president's remarks, emphasizing the broader stakes for the region.

"This is an attack not just on one man, but on the very idea of a free, independent, and democratic Lebanon," Rice said during a press briefing. "The international community will not stand by while those who seek stability and self-determination are targeted for assassination. We urge all parties to allow justice to take its course."

At the United Nations, the secretary-general issued a statement calling for calm and unity.

"I am deeply saddened and outraged by this cowardly act of violence," the secretary-general said. "I call upon all Lebanese to remain united in the face of those who wish to sow division and chaos. The United Nations reaffirms its commitment to supporting Lebanon's sovereignty, stability, and the rule of law. Those responsible for this crime must be brought to justice."

## Political Fallout

The killing has intensified an already tense political climate, with opposition figures accusing external forces of orchestrating the attack to intimidate dissenting voices. Government officials have called for restraint while pledging a thorough investigation, and some have signaled openness to international assistance in the inquiry.

Analysts warn that the assassination could deepen sectarian tensions and complicate ongoing efforts to stabilize the country's delicate power-sharing arrangement.

"This is a pivotal moment," said a regional political analyst based in Beirut. "How the government and the international community respond in the coming weeks will determine whether Lebanon moves toward accountability or slides back into cycles of violence."

## Calls for Justice

As the funeral procession concluded, family members of the slain politician urged mourners to channel their grief into peaceful resolve.

"We will not seek revenge," a relative told the crowd. "We seek truth, and we seek justice."

Security forces remained on high alert throughout the capital, with additional checkpoints established near government buildings and foreign embassies. Officials have not yet named any suspects, though investigators say they are pursuing several leads.

The Lebanese government has declared a period of national mourning, and flags across the country flew at half-staff.

# Bomb Kills Anti-Syrian Lawmaker as Lebanon Braces for Divisive Presidential Vote

**BEIRUT** — A powerful car bomb tore through a Christian neighborhood of Beirut on Wednesday, killing an anti-Syrian member of parliament and several bystanders, in the latest assassination to shake Lebanon as the deeply divided nation approaches a critical vote to choose a new president.

The blast, which struck during the afternoon rush in the Sin el-Fil district, killed the lawmaker along with at least six other people and wounded dozens more. Charred vehicles and shattered glass littered the street as rescue workers pulled victims from the wreckage and ambulances raced through the panicked crowds.

The killing marks the latest in a string of assassinations targeting prominent critics of Syrian influence in Lebanon over the past two years, deepening a political crisis that has paralyzed the country and raised fears of renewed sectarian conflict.

## A Pattern of Violence

The attack fits a grim pattern that began with the massive truck bombing that killed former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in February 2005. That assassination triggered the "Cedar Revolution," mass protests that ultimately forced Syria to withdraw its troops after nearly three decades of military presence in Lebanon.

Since then, a series of journalists, politicians, and public figures associated with the anti-Syrian March 14 coalition have been killed or targeted in bombings and shootings. Each attack has further narrowed the parliamentary majority held by the governing coalition, led by Hariri's son Saad and backed by Western and Sunni Arab governments.

Members of the March 14 alliance were quick to blame Syria and its Lebanese allies for the latest killing, accusations that Damascus has repeatedly and firmly denied.

"This is a systematic campaign to decapitate the free voices of Lebanon," said one coalition figure, who called the assassination "a message aimed at the heart of our democracy."

## The Presidential Stakes

The timing of the attack is especially significant. Lebanon's parliament is scheduled to convene in the coming weeks to elect a successor to President Émile Lahoud, whose term is set to expire. Lahoud, a pro-Syrian figure, has been a central point of contention in the political standoff.

Under Lebanon's confessional system, the presidency is reserved for a Maronite Christian, while the prime minister must be a Sunni Muslim and the speaker of parliament a Shiite. The presidential election requires a two-thirds quorum in the 128-seat parliament, giving the opposition — led by the Shiite movement Hezbollah and its Christian allies — the power to block a vote by boycotting the session.

The March 14 coalition holds a slim majority, but each assassination erodes their numbers further. With razor-thin margins, the loss of even a single lawmaker carries outsized weight, and the killing intensifies suspicions that violence is being used to alter the political arithmetic.

## Deadlock and Fears of a Vacuum

The competing blocs have been unable to agree on a compromise candidate, raising the prospect of a dangerous constitutional vacuum should the presidency fall vacant with no successor in place. Some fear the emergence of two rival governments, a scenario that would echo the chaos of Lebanon's 1975–1990 civil war.

The opposition insists on a "national unity" arrangement that would grant it veto power in the cabinet, while the governing coalition accuses its rivals of trying to impose Syrian and Iranian interests on the country. International mediators, including French and Arab League envoys, have shuttled between the factions in hopes of brokering a deal.

## Regional Shadows

The crisis in Lebanon reflects broader regional tensions, with the country serving as a battleground for influence between the United States and its allies on one side, and Syria and Iran on the other. Washington has thrown its support behind the March 14 government, while accusing Damascus of destabilizing its smaller neighbor.

A United Nations tribunal investigating the Hariri assassination and subsequent killings has added to the pressure on Syria, and Wednesday's attack is likely to fall within its expanding mandate.

## A Nation on Edge
